crm_note.headline: Rohan completed the Fernhallow final round; Fernhallow does not buy out garden leave and a prop shop offer is expected in the week of the call
crm_note.how_it_went: Rohan described the round as "Good, I think, but long". It ran to three hours because Marcus Elling kept him for an extra chat at the end, which Rohan took as a good sign. In the presentation, Marcus said "OK, good" after Rohan showed his factor-neutral backup slide, and Rohan took that as high praise.

rounds.format: A 30-minute presentation of a past project (sanitised earnings drift work, with no Sallowmere numbers), followed by questioning for the second half of the hour. Present were Marcus Elling (PM) and two researchers, Nadia and Felix.
asked: Is this just value in disguise: has the signal been neutralised against the standard factors, or is it a value tilt?
What would make you kill this signal: what evidence, what threshold, would you switch it off live?
How long would you wait: would you sit through six months of drawdown?
Why does it work economically, and who is on the other side of the trade?
rounds.candidate_view: Marcus interrupted at slide three. Rohan had a backup slide with the factor-neutral version, where the effect drops but is still there. He took Marcus's "OK, good" as high praise. On the kill-signal question, he said he would rather cut the size than kill the signal outright, and would set the rule before going live; Felix nodded a lot at that. Rohan said Marcus clearly hates "the model found it" answers.

rounds.format: 30 minutes with Ingrid Saarinen, head of research
asked: Culture and how he likes to work
How he deals with being wrong
Whether he would be willing to ask his firm to shorten the notice and non-compete
rounds.candidate_view: Rohan described this session as much softer. Ingrid told him Fernhallow does not buy out garden leave, as a policy. She said they are used to waiting and it is not a deal-breaker. Rohan said he would try to get his firm to shorten it.

rounds.format: 15 minutes, one to one, at the end of the day
rounds.candidate_view: Rohan said Marcus did not flinch at his figures. He noted that nobody had asked him for references before an offer until now; Hannah told him Fernhallow normally takes references early.

compensation.expectation: Base £180k and a bonus that reflects the PnL
compensation.notes: Rohan gave these figures to Marcus Elling in the extra chat. He asked Hannah to find out whether Fernhallow would guarantee his year one bonus, which would make the garden leave easier to accept. Hannah said she would ask, with no promises. Marcus also asked for references.

crm_note.notice_and_non_compete: Notice is 12 weeks and the non-compete is 6 months, so close to nine months before he could start if Sallowmere enforces both fully. Fernhallow does not buy out garden leave, as a policy. Ingrid said they are used to waiting and it is not a deal-breaker, and asked whether Rohan would ask his firm to shorten it. He said he would try.
competing_processes: A prop shop has said it will make Rohan an offer in the week of the call, with a higher guaranteed bonus. Rohan said he would still rather Fernhallow. Hannah will not share this with Fernhallow unless Rohan wants her to use it.
risks: The prop shop offer is expected in the week of the call and carries a higher guaranteed bonus.
Start date of close to nine months if Sallowmere enforces the full 12 weeks' notice and 6 months' non-compete, and Fernhallow will not buy out garden leave.
Rohan is worried about a counter-offer conversation with his boss, who he expects to take it personally.

next_actions.action: Speak to Ingrid Saarinen to get a read on the final round
Ask Fernhallow whether they would guarantee Rohan's year one bonus (no promises given)
Come straight back to Rohan after speaking to Ingrid
next_actions.due: straight after speaking to Ingrid (said on the call)

next_actions.action: Try to get Sallowmere to shorten his notice and non-compete

candidate.subject: Fernhallow final round: next steps
candidate.body:
Hi Rohan,

Thanks for taking the time to talk me through the final round at Fernhallow today.

I will speak to Ingrid tomorrow to get a read, and I will come straight back to you after that. I will also ask whether Fernhallow would guarantee your year one bonus. I can't promise anything on that, but I will ask.

I won't share the other offer with Fernhallow unless you want me to use it.

On your side, you said you would try asking Sallowmere to shorten your notice and non-compete.

Thanks again, and speak soon.

Best wishes,
Hannah

client.subject: Rohan Mehta: final round
client.body:
Hi Ingrid,

Thank you for interviewing Rohan Mehta for the Quantitative Researcher, Systematic Equities role.

Rohan remains interested in the role.

I would be grateful for your feedback on the final round, and I would be glad to hear your thoughts on next steps. I will give you a call tomorrow.

Best wishes,
Hannah

process.format: Video call, about 45 minutes. About ten minutes on your CV, then probability questions typed into a shared document. No code.
process.who: Graham Lowe, senior researcher. He gives very little feedback during the call, mostly "OK, next one".
process.what_they_look_for: Checking your own answers, and how you validated past work: out-of-sample testing and holdout choice rather than the headline Sharpe.

process.format: At the office. First hour: one probability warm-up question, then live Python on a firm laptop with no internet, using deliberately messy daily price and volume data. Second hour: a backtest critique case.
process.who: Nadia Osei, a researcher on the equities side, for the first hour. Nadia and another researcher, Pieter (surname not caught), for the case.
process.what_they_look_for: Sound logic over exact syntax, spotting data problems such as series that stop part way through, and a thorough critique of a backtest including trading costs and market impact.

process.format: Research presentation on a past project of your choice that you can discuss without breaking confidentiality: 30 minutes presenting, with questions taking the presentation and questions to about an hour together. Then 30 minutes with the head of research. The final also included an extra 15-minute chat with the PM and took about three hours in total.
process.who: Marcus Elling (PM) and two researchers, Nadia and Felix, for the presentation. Ingrid Saarinen, head of research, for the second part. Marcus for the extra chat.
process.what_they_look_for: Whether a signal survives neutralising against standard factors, an economic reason it works (who is on the other side of the trade), and clear rules for when to switch a signal off. With Ingrid: culture, how you like to work and how you deal with being wrong.

examples: Expected number of rolls of a fair die until you see a six
Expected number of coin flips until you get two heads in a row
The same question for heads followed by tails
Three random points on a circle: probability the triangle contains the centre
A stick broken at two random points: probability the three pieces make a triangle

question_themes.theme: Deep dive on past research and its validation
examples: How you handle momentum crash periods such as 2009
Whether the work was tested out of sample properly or tuned on the whole history

question_themes.theme: Live Python on messy equity data
examples: Build a simple reversal signal on daily prices and volumes for a few hundred stocks over about ten years, and say what the performance looks like
"What's wrong with this" about a backtest with a Sharpe of about 2.1
How many variants had been tried to get this one
How you would model market impact for small caps, and what participation rate
"Is this just value in disguise": have you neutralised against the standard factors?
"What would make you kill this signal": what evidence, what threshold, would you switch it off live?
How long would you wait: would you sit through six months of drawdown?
Why does it work economically, and who is on the other side of the trade?
How you deal with being wrong

went_well: On two heads in a row, giving four first, then correcting to six and walking through the states, drew "good, you checked it" from Graham.
Not recalling exact groupby syntax, saying "I'd normally check the docs here" and writing the intended logic in pseudo-pandas: Nadia said that was fine and that she cares about the logic.
Asking, before computing anything, why some series end (delisted or acquired), because dropping them creates survivorship bias, drew a smile from Nadia.
When Marcus asked at slide three whether the effect was just value in disguise, a backup slide with the factor-neutral version (the effect drops but is still there) drew "OK, good" from him.
On when to kill a signal, cutting the size rather than killing it outright, with the rule set before going live and not after, drew a lot of nodding from Felix.
tripped_people_up: Citing a holdout from 2019 onwards drew a follow-up from Graham on who chose the holdout.
In the backtest case the interviewers pushed hard on costs: how to model market impact for small caps and what participation rate to assume. The answer on this was hand-wavy.
advice: For your second round, expect one probability question at the start of the Python hour. Practise classics such as the broken stick and random points on a circle, and say plainly if you have seen one before.
With no internet on the laptop, if you cannot recall exact pandas syntax, say so and write the logic clearly. Nadia has said the logic is what she cares about.
Inspect the data before building the signal: ask why series stop, and deal with gaps and bad prints, so you do not introduce survivorship bias.
For the backtest case, cover look-ahead (trading at the same close used for the signal), turnover and costs, and multiple testing, including deflating the Sharpe for the number of trials.
Prepare a concrete market impact approach for small caps, with participation rates, as costs have drawn the most pressure in the case.
On probability questions, check your answer aloud before moving on. Correcting yourself has drawn praise.
For the final, bring a factor-neutral backup slide, an economic story for who is on the other side of the trade, and a kill rule you would set before going live.
logistics: The second round is at the office, on a laptop the firm provides with no internet access.
Feedback after the technical round usually takes a few days.

Notice period and non-compete have been asked about in every round: by Graham at the end of the first round, by Nadia in the second round and by Ingrid in the final. Your record shows 8 weeks' notice and a 3-month non-compete, so have these ready.
Ingrid stated it is company policy that the firm does not buy out garden leave.
For the final presentation you can use any past project you can discuss without breaking confidentiality, with real figures removed.
Marcus asked for references at the final, before any offer.
